classification_signals: Title explicitly states 'A novel theory explains why the brain craves information'
Authors state 'Here we present a hypothesis for how this mechanism works.' (p. 2)

Paper describes their own empirical studies (behavioral preference ratings, fMRI) as evidence supporting the proposed theory, rather than being the primary focus of detailed empirical reporting (e.g., 'In our experiments, we presented a series of images...' p. 6)
Discussion focuses on the implications and further development of the theory.
title: Perceptual Pleasure and the Brain: A novel theory explains why the brain craves information and seeks it through the senses
authors: Irving Biederman and Edward A. Vessel, 2006

findings.antecedent: Acquiring information (novel, richly interpretable visual stimuli)
findings.quote: We believe that the enjoyment of such experiences is deeply connected to an innate hunger for information: Human beings are designed to be 'infovores.'

findings.antecedent: Position along ventral visual pathway (from early stages V1-V4 to later stages parahippocampal/rhinal cortex)
findings.quote: the receptors are distributed in a gradient that gradually increases in density along the so-called ventral visual pathway

findings.antecedent: Visual stimulus containing a great deal of interpretable information (eliciting many episodic or semantic memories)
findings.consequent: Neural activity in association areas, release of endomorphins, stimulation of mu-opioid receptors, pleasant effects
findings.quote: If a stimulus contains a great deal of interpretable information, it should lead to more neural activity in the association areas and hence to a greater release of endomorphins
With each repetition, their preference for an image declined.

findings.antecedent: Repeated presentation of a stimulus pattern (due to competitive learning and inhibition of weakly engaged neurons)
findings.consequent: Net activity of neurons in visual association areas
findings.quote: repetition results in a net reduction of neural activity.

findings.consequent: fMRI activity in ventral occipito-temporal cortex (collateral sulcus and adjacent parahippocampal cortex)
findings.quote: the activity in a portion of the ventral occipito-temporal cortex... declined with each repeated presentation.

findings.antecedent: Scenes rated as highly preferred (or interesting)
findings.consequent: fMRI activity in parahippocampal cortex (visual association areas)
findings.quote: scenes that were rated highly elicited the most fMRI activity in the parahippocampal cortex

findings.antecedent: Scene features (broad views of landscape, hidden vantage point, element of mystery, natural settings)
findings.quote: Preferred pictures often contained broad views of the landscape, especially scenes that provided a hidden vantage point

findings.antecedent: Simple visual pattern (droodle) + caption (making it interpretable/funny)
findings.quote: Reading the droodle's caption makes it funny, because the reader activates a train of associations that reconcile what is otherwise a meaningless pattern.

findings.antecedent: Repeated exposure to a stimulus that is not yet understood (e.g., new idea, challenging subject matter)
findings.consequent: Pleasure / preference (peaking at 'click' of comprehension, then declining)
findings.quote: as one struggles to comprehend a new idea, there is increased pleasure with repeated exposure, which peaks at what has been called the 'click' of comprehension.

findings.antecedent: Position along auditory system (primary auditory cortex vs. secondary auditory cortex)
findings.quote: Here the receptors are relatively sparse in the primary auditory cortex and denser in the secondary auditory cortex.

findings.antecedent: Listening to stirring music + receiving naloxone (mu-opioid antagonist)
findings.quote: people who normally experienced 'chills' while listening to certain stirring pieces of music did not have the same sensations when they received the drug naloxone

limitations: Incomplete understanding of the full reward pathway, specifically the next stages after opioid release and their connection to dopamine in the corpus striatum (p. 5).
Exceptions to the novelty preference, particularly in childhood behavior like video games, suggesting other reward systems might be at play (p. 7).
Primary focus on the visual system, with the generalizability to other sensory systems being a suspicion rather than proven (p. 8).
General acknowledgment that 'much that remains to be explained about the human obsession with information' (p. 8).
minimum_safe_summary: This paper proposes a novel 'infovore' theory, suggesting the brain inherently craves information, which is rewarded by the release of natural opioids. The theory posits that interpretable and novel visual stimuli activate mu-opioid receptors in visual association areas, particularly the parahippocampal cortex, leading to pleasure. Empirical fMRI studies described by the authors support this by showing increased activity in these areas for highly preferred and novel scenes, with activity declining upon repeated exposure due to competitive learning. The authors acknowledge limitations, including the full extent of the reward pathway and exceptions to novelty preference in certain contexts like childhood play.
